question: What is the primary focus of palliative care?

options.A: Improving the quality of life for patients and their families
options.B: Replacing all traditional medical treatments with herbal remedies
options.C: Accelerating the natural dying process through medication
options.D: Finding a permanent cure for terminal infectious diseases

explanation: Palliative care specifically aims to enhance quality of life by preventing and relieving suffering for both the patient and their loved ones during serious illness. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h1)

question: When can palliative care be introduced during the course of a serious illness?

options.A: At any stage alongside life-prolonging treatments
options.B: Exclusively after all curative options have failed
options.C: Only when the patient is discharged back home
options.D: Only during the final twenty-four hours of life

explanation: Palliative care is not just for end-of-life; it can and should be integrated early alongside disease-modifying or curative treatments. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h1)

question: How does palliative care view the dying process?

options.A: As a medical failure that must be avoided
options.B: As a punishment for past misdeeds
options.C: As a condition that can always be reversed
options.D: As a normal and natural part of life

explanation: Palliative care philosophy regards dying as a normal human process that neither hastens nor postpones death. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h2)

question: Why is the family considered a primary unit of care in palliative care?

options.A: They are responsible for administering strong narcotics.
options.B: They pay the hospital bills directly out of pocket.
options.C: They experience the burden of illness and need support too.
options.D: They make all medical decisions without the patient.

explanation: Because a serious illness affects the entire family unit, palliative care extends support to relatives during the illness and through bereavement. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h2)

question: What is the main difference between curative treatment and palliative care?

options.A: Curative treatment aims to eradicate disease, while palliative care focuses on comfort and quality of life.
options.B: Curative treatment is only for the elderly, while palliative care is for young children.
options.C: Curative treatment ignores physical pain, while palliative care focuses only on surgery.
options.D: Curative treatment is provided at home, while palliative care requires an intensive care unit.

explanation: Think of it this way: curative treatment fights the disease itself to get rid of it, while palliative care fights the discomfort and pain so the patient can feel better day-to-day. You've got this! [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h3)

question: A patient with lung cancer is still getting chemotherapy while also receiving care for severe pain and shortness of breath. What kind of approach is this?

options.A: Integrating palliative care alongside curative treatment
options.B: Treating the side effects of chemotherapy exclusively with surgery
options.C: Abandoning curative treatment in favor of hospice
options.D: Stopping all medical interventions to allow natural death

explanation: Brilliant! Patients don't have to choose just one. They can receive treatments to fight the illness (like chemotherapy) while simultaneously getting comfort care to manage their symptoms. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h3)

question: Why do we need a team of different professionals in palliative care?

options.A: Hospital regulations require at least ten staff members per patient.
options.B: No single profession can address all physical, emotional, and spiritual needs.
options.C: Nurses only handle administrative paperwork in palliative settings.
options.D: Doctors are not allowed to talk to family members directly.

explanation: No single person knows it all! Caring for someone with a serious illness takes doctors, nurses, social workers, and spiritual leaders all working hand-in-hand to cover every angle. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h4)

question: A patient with terminal cancer is stressed about hospital bills and how their children will eat. Which team member is best suited to help with this?
explanation: Spot on! Social workers are absolute champions at helping families navigate financial worries, connect with community resources, and handle practical support. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h4)

question: In clinical nursing, how do we truly know how much pain a patient is in?

options.A: Pain only exists if visible tissue damage is present.
options.B: Pain is whatever the experiencing patient says it is.
options.C: Pain is a psychological illusion created by anxiety.
options.D: Pain can be accurately measured solely by high blood pressure.

explanation: Remember this golden rule of nursing: pain is subjective. If the patient says it hurts, it hurts! Always trust and validate your patient's report. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h5)

question: Why must nurses look at the whole person—not just physical symptoms—when caring for palliative patients?

options.A: Physical pain never occurs without accompanying fever.
options.B: Physical symptoms are often worsened by emotional and spiritual distress.
options.C: Medications only work if the patient is sleeping soundly.
options.D: Lab tests can detect all forms of human suffering.

explanation: Everything is connected! When a patient is worried, scared, or spiritually troubled, their physical pain often feels much worse. Holistic care means healing the whole person. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT part of a holistic palliative assessment?

options.A: Respecting cultural beliefs and family traditions
options.B: Strictly monitoring laboratory blood cell counts
options.D: Listening to spiritual and existential concerns

explanation: While lab results matter in acute care, palliative care is all about the human experience—feelings, culture, and spirit. It's much more than just numbers on a lab sheet! [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h6)

question: Why is cultural awareness so vital when providing end-of-life care in Nigeria?

options.A: Foreign medications only work if combined with local herbs.
options.B: Standard hospital guidelines override all traditional practices automatically.
options.C: Cultural rituals prevent patients from feeling any physical pain.
options.D: Cultural beliefs deeply influence how families view death, dying, and mourning.

explanation: Culture shapes how our patients and their families understand illness and say goodbye. Respecting this helps us provide compassionate, dignified nursing care. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h6)

question: Which sign do we often see when a patient is in the final active dying phase?

options.A: Warm, flushed skin over the entire body
options.B: Irregular breathing patterns like Cheyne-Stokes respirations
options.C: Rapid increase in blood pressure and heart rate
options.D: Sudden increase in appetite and high energy levels

explanation: As the body gently slows down, you might notice cool hands and feet, sleeping more, and irregular breathing patterns like Cheyne-Stokes. Knowing this helps you reassure the family. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of bereavement support after a patient passes away?

options.A: To disinfect the hospital room according to policy
options.B: To complete hospital discharge billing procedures quickly
options.C: To help surviving family members process their grief and cope with loss
options.D: To determine the exact legal cause of death for insurance

explanation: Bereavement support extends palliative care principles to the family after death, assisting them through the normal grieving process. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h7)

question: What is a major challenge nurses often face when providing palliative care in resource-limited settings?

options.A: An excess of high-tech equipment that overwhelms patients
options.B: Limited access to essential pain medications and specialized facilities
options.C: A complete absence of family involvement in patient care
options.D: Patients refusing all forms of basic nursing assessment

explanation: In many resource-constrained settings, getting a steady supply of pain relief like opioids can be tough. Nigerian nurses often have to be creative and strong advocates for their patients! [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h8)

question: A family is hesitant to discuss a terminal diagnosis with their elderly parent due to cultural traditions. As a nurse, what is your best first step?

options.A: Explore the family's cultural concerns and work collaboratively to honor their values while ensuring patient comfort
options.B: Report the family to hospital security for withholding medical information
options.C: Ignore the family and tell the patient the diagnosis immediately without warning
options.D: Discontinue all palliative support until the family changes their tradition

explanation: Great nursing requires teamwork with the family! By listening to their cultural perspectives, you can find a respectful way forward that keeps the patient comfortable and honored. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T1#GNS321_U4_T1_h8)
